case_study_insert.main_stem: Portview Valves & Fittings (PVF) is a public limited company in the industrial fluid-control sector, employing a workforce of 60. Founded in 1999 by Jonas Portview, who remains chief executive, it makes brass valves and pipe fittings for water utilities and chemical plants, and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. PVF plans to invest $1,100,000 in an automated valve-testing facility, financed by a $700,000 new share issue and $400,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $360,000 a year, a variable cost of $12.00 a unit and a selling price of $20.00, and currently produces 90,000 units a year. PVF faces two operational problems: a defect rate of 2.8% in pressure testing and rising complaints about delivery reliability from utility clients.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Report — Q3 2025: The test facility checked 21,600 valves last quarter at a defect rate of 2.8%, down from 4.0% a year ago. Late deliveries fell from 48 to 26 a month, and average lead time is 6.2 days. A survey of 380 procurement managers found 66% would pay up to $0.80 more for certified pressure-tested valves and 55% require test certificates before ordering. Training records show 16 of 60 assembly workers have not completed on-the-job training on the new test benches; external accreditation courses cost $920 per employee.
case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing debt-service costs. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.0% from $13.49 to $14.30 an hour from April 2026. (3) Brass and stainless-steel input costs have risen 10.5% year-on-year, energy price inflation is 7.2%, and European industrial production expanded 2.1% over the same period.

questions.question_text: PVF plans to raise $700,000 through a new share issue to fund its $1,100,000 valve-testing facility. Explain two advantages for PVF of a share issue compared with a bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A share issue brings in $700,000 of permanent capital with no interest charges or compulsory repayments, so PVF does not add debt service to its $360,000 a year fixed costs while it equips the $1,100,000 testing facility. That protects the $8.00 contribution on each of 90,000 valves and leaves the $400,000 retained profit free for working capital as utility clients demand more reliable deliveries.

Point 2: Because PVF is a public limited company, a share issue can raise a large sum from many investors and spread the risk of the new facility beyond Jonas Portview's existing shareholders. Unlike borrowing, there is no collateral to pledge and no lender covenants, giving management freedom to set testing standards and respond to the 2.8% defect rate, while the 66% of surveyed buyers willing to pay $0.80 more for certified valves offer a return that can justify the new investment.

Shareholders also expect a return through dividends or rising value, so PVF must earn that $8.00 contribution on enough of its 90,000 units to keep the share price stable.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue (max 2).
1 mark for each valid advantage of a share issue (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PVF's capital, contribution and expansion.
Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to PVF's risk, control and survey evidence.

questions.question_text: PVF is promoting its new certified pressure-tested valves. Consider print advertising in engineering trade journals, sponsoring an industry exhibition, or e-commerce and digital marketing. Which should PVF choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Print advertising in trade journals: Engineering magazines reach the procurement managers PVF supplies and can carry the message that 66% of 380 surveyed buyers would pay $0.80 more for certified valves. But circulation is limited, adverts must be repeated to work, and a page cannot provide the test certificates the 55% require, so a 60-employee company funding a $1,100,000 facility may see weak returns.

Industry exhibition sponsorship: A stand lets water-utility and chemical-plant buyers inspect valves and ask about certification, directly answering the 55% who need certificates and helping offset a 2.8% defect rate with visible quality. Yet stand, travel and staffing costs are high, the event is short and geographically concentrated, and it may not generate the steady order flow needed to use 90,000 units of capacity.

E-commerce and digital marketing: A website can publish certificates online, target procurement managers by sector and record enquiries, so the 55% who require test documents are served instantly and the 66% premium message is measured against orders. It scales nationally without exhibition costs and suits the 6.2-day lead time, although it needs ongoing digital investment and search visibility before results build.

Recommendation: PVF should choose e-commerce and digital marketing. It delivers certification evidence to the exact surveyed segment at controllable cost and can be tracked against 90,000-unit output. Trade journals are rejected as narrow and unmeasurable; the exhibition is rejected as costly and short-lived. A small exhibition presence can be added later if digital leads justify it.

PVF should monitor enquiries from water utilities against the 6.2-day lead time so the marketing spend translates into orders rather than unfulfilled interest.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to PVF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of PVF with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of PVF and recommends e-commerce, explaining why trade journals and the exhibition are rejected.

questions.question_text: PVF's flat structure and laissez-faire leadership coexist with a 2.8% defect rate and late deliveries. Explain two benefits for PVF of introducing team working in its assembly area.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Team working pools the skills of the 60 assembly workers so they can jointly diagnose the 2.8% pressure-testing defect rate, using the practical knowledge of the 16 of 60 workers awaiting on-the-job training on new test benches. Shared responsibility gives the team ownership of quality, which suits PVF's flat structure and can cut the 21,600 valves checked each quarter that need rework.

Point 2: Working in teams satisfies social needs and, through Herzberg's motivators of responsibility and recognition, raises effort on delivery reliability as late deliveries have fallen from 48 to 26 but remain a complaint. Teams can cover for absent colleagues, protecting the $8.00 contribution on 90,000 units, and the $920 accreditation courses can be delivered to groups, spreading the cost across the team rather than individuals.

Team leaders should be chosen from workers already trained on the test benches, so guidance on the 2.8% defect rate is reliable, and the flat structure allows their ideas to reach Jonas Portview without delay.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit of team working (max 2).
1 mark for each valid benefit of team working (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to PVF's defect rate, training and deliveries.
Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation linked to PVF's motivation, output and costs.

questions.question_text: PVF must improve motivation among assembly workers to cut pressure-test defects. Consider a financial bonus or job enrichment. Which should PVF choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
Financial bonus: A payment tied to output or defect targets gives an immediate, visible reward and can quickly raise effort on the 21,600 valves checked each quarter, which would help cut the 2.8% defect rate and the $920-per-person training bill. However, a bonus focused on speed may encourage workers to rush pressure tests and hide faults, worsening quality for the 55% of buyers who require certificates, and it adds a recurring cost to $360,000 fixed costs without building lasting skill.

Job enrichment: Giving assembly workers responsibility for running the new test benches and signing off certificates expands their job content and satisfies Herzberg's motivators of responsibility and achievement, which suits PVF's flat structure and laissez-faire leadership. It builds ownership of quality and can sustain a lower defect rate, but it requires the 16 of 60 workers to complete on-the-job training and $920 courses, so benefits appear more slowly than a bonus.

Decision: PVF should choose job enrichment. It attacks the cause of the 2.8% defect rate by giving workers control over testing, and its cost is a one-off training investment rather than a permanent bonus bill. A pure financial bonus is rejected because it could reward volume over the certified quality that 55% of buyers demand; PVF can add a small quality-linked bonus only after certificate standards are embedded.

PVF can pilot job enrichment with one team on the new test benches, measure the 2.8% defect rate after a quarter, and only then extend it across the 60 assembly workers. This staged approach limits risk while the $920 accreditation courses are rolled out, and it fits the flat structure better than a universal bonus scheme would.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Describes the two motivation methods with limited application to PVF.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of PVF.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates both methods in the context of PVF and makes a justified decision that rejects a pure bonus, covering quality, training and motivation theory.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how PVF's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $360,000 ÷ ($20.00 − $12.00) = $360,000 ÷ $8.00 = 45,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 45,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $20.00 − $12.00 = $8.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $8.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways PVF's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare break-even of 45,000 units with output of 90,000 units: the margin of safety is 45,000 units, showing the cushion if utility orders slip.
2. Use the $8.00 contribution to price the $0.80 certification premium and judge whether extra testing for the 2.8% defect rate is covered.
3. Check that contribution on 90,000 units can justify the $700,000 share issue and the $1,100,000 facility, setting volume targets for Jonas Portview.
4. Track unit cost of $360,000 ÷ 90,000 + $12.00 = $16.00 to detect waste from testing rework and the 10.5% brass price rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 45,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $8.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety 45,000 units; certification premium pricing; share-issue viability; and unit-cost benchmarking at $16.00.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and 1 mark for the accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark for each valid applied use in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate PVF's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has PVF's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.49 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.64 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.89 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 1.09 : 1

Detailed workings: In 2024 current assets were $210,000 inventories + $240,000 trade receivables + $70,000 cash = $520,000, and $520,000 ÷ $350,000 current liabilities gives the 2024 measure. In 2025 the corresponding assets were $180,000 + $265,000 + $95,000 = $540,000, and $540,000 ÷ $330,000 gives the 2025 measure. For the stock-excluding measure the 2024 numerator is $520,000 − $210,000 = $310,000, and $310,000 ÷ $350,000 = 0.89; in 2025 $540,000 − $180,000 = $360,000 and $360,000 ÷ $330,000 = 1.09.

Evaluation: Liquidity has improved. The broad coverage measure rose from 1.49 to 1.64 as current liabilities fell from $350,000 to $330,000 and cash rose from $70,000 to $95,000. The stock-excluding measure also improved, from 0.89 to 1.09, so PVF is less dependent on selling valves from inventory to meet short-term debts — useful while it funds a $1,100,000 facility. The concern is trade receivables rising from $240,000 to $265,000; if utility clients pay slowly, the stronger position could weaken, and lower inventories of $180,000 may need watching given 6.2-day lead times.

Conclusion: PVF's financial position has improved. Both the 2024–2025 measures (1.49 to 1.64 and 0.89 to 1.09) rose and the gain does not rely on stock. The residual risk is higher receivables, so tighter credit control should accompany the new investment.

With $540,000 of current assets against $330,000 of current liabilities, PVF has enough headroom to absorb a short dip in utility receipts while the testing facility is commissioned.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current and acid test measures for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventory, receivables and liabilities movements and a justified conclusion on whether PVF's position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for PVF of introducing robotics into its valve-testing facility.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Robots can repeat pressure tests consistently, cutting the 2.8% defect rate and reducing rework on the 21,600 valves checked last quarter, which protects the $8.00 contribution on each of 90,000 units. Consistent digital records also support the test certificates wanted by 55% of buyers and the $0.80 premium accepted by 66%, strengthening the case for the $1,100,000 facility.

Disadvantage: Robotics adds capital cost on top of the $1,100,000 already committed and raises fixed costs above $360,000 a year, pushing the 45,000-unit break-even higher if demand from water utilities dips. The 16 of 60 workers still awaiting on-the-job training may need $920 accreditation courses to supervise the robots, and automation could demotivate staff in a flat structure that currently relies on laissez-faire leadership and team-based problem solving.

PVF should introduce robotics alongside the $920 accreditation courses so the 16 of 60 workers still untrained can supervise the machines, and should trial one cell first to check that the 2.8% defect rate really falls before committing the whole $1,100,000 facility.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage of robotics.
1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage of robotics.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PVF's defect rate, certificates and contribution.
Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to PVF's break-even, training and motivation.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.25%, the 6.0% minimum wage increase and the 10.5% rise in brass and stainless-steel input costs will affect PVF. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): PVF's new facility is funded by a $700,000 share issue and $400,000 retained profit, so this plan carries no new bank-loan interest. Higher base rates may still make investors demand better returns from the share issue and slow utility clients' capital spending, but no direct interest cost on PVF's existing finance can be invented from the insert, so the effect is indirect and limited.

Minimum wage increase (6.0%, to $14.30 an hour): PVF employs 60 workers and the rise lifts its wage bill, but the insert gives no hours worked or pay rates, so a total cannot be calculated honestly. The defensible comparison is productivity: 90,000 units ÷ 60 staff = 1,500 units per worker. Unless that holds or output grows, unit labour cost rises and erodes the $8.00 contribution per valve.

Input cost inflation (10.5% brass and stainless steel): The $12.00 variable cost is not decomposed in the insert, so only a bound is possible — if the entire variable cost rose 10.5% it would add 0.105 × $12.00 = $1.26 a unit, or 90,000 × $1.26 = $113,400 a year. Even a smaller rise squeezes the 45,000-unit break-even, though the $0.80 premium accepted by 66% of buyers gives partial protection.

Conclusion: The 10.5% rise in brass and steel costs will have the greatest impact. It compounds across all 90,000 valves and directly threatens the $8.00 contribution that underpins the $1,100,000 investment. The interest-rate effect is indirect with no stated loan, and the wage effect depends on productivity, so neither is as pervasive as material inflation.
